APRA's May 2026 settings retain a three-percentage-point mortgage serviceability buffer. This is an ADI prudential requirement, not a claim that every lender or loan in Australia follows an identical assessment.

With an assumed 6.19% rate, adding three points gives 9.19%. On AUD 520,000 over 25 years, the monthly model gives AUD 3,411.02 at 6.19% and AUD 4,431.68 at 9.19%. The difference is assessment headroom, not a fee added to the actual loan payment.

Australia DTI: The High-Debt Lending Limit in Force Since February 2026
Publisher contact: Abdul RaheemPublisher: REO TechnologiesUpdated: October 25, 2026

Australia's high-DTI framework is now more than monitoring. From February 1, 2026, APRA limits the share of new lending at debt-to-income ratios greater than or equal to six. That limits a lender's high-debt business; it does not make six a personal statutory borrowing maximum.

A basic ratio is total assessed debt divided by gross annual qualifying income. With AUD 520,000 mortgage debt, no other debt and AUD 95,000 income, the simple result is 5.47 times. Adding AUD 50,000 assessed other debt gives 6.00 times. Exactly six is within APRA's high-DTI category, not below it.

APRA's activation notice permits up to 20% of new owner-occupier lending and separately up to 20% of new investment lending at DTI of six or more, subject to its scope and implementation requirements. The May 2026 settings review maintained the settings.

Publisher contact: Abdul RaheemPublisher: REO TechnologiesUpdated: October 26, 2026

A bigger down payment reduces the loan, but it also leaves less cash in your account after closing. Comparing the monthly saving with the extra cash committed is more useful than treating 20% as a target everyone must reach.

Some conventional programs permit 3% down for eligible buyers. Eligibility can depend on income, property use, education and first-time-buyer status. Fannie Mae's down-payment overview distinguishes HomeReady from its standard 97% financing option; not every 3%-down program has identical rules.

At 5% or 10% down, principal is lower and PMI pricing may differ, but the premium depends on the borrower and product. At 20% down on a typical conventional purchase, borrower-paid monthly PMI is generally unnecessary. That threshold does not waive FHA mortgage insurance, establish loan approval or guarantee the best note rate.

This example holds price at $412,500, rate at 7.32%, and term at 30 years. The rate is an illustrative use of the October 22, 2026 Freddie Mac benchmark cited in the mortgage guide. Each PMI rate below is an explicitly chosen scenario input, not a current market average.

Moving from 3% to 20% down commits an additional $70,125 and lowers the modeled P&I-plus-PMI cost by $791.81 a month. Some of that difference repays a smaller principal balance and some avoids the assumed insurance charge. It is not a simple investment return or a permanent saving: PMI may end, and actual quotes may use different rates.

A $41,250 down payment does not mean $41,250 is the total cash needed. Lender charges, appraisal and title costs, prepaid insurance and initial escrow can add to cash to close. Seller credits, deposits already paid and assistance programs can change it too. Use the lender's Loan Estimate rather than a fixed national percentage to settle the budget.

For many covered conventional loans, a written cancellation request at 80% of original value has payment-history, lien and value conditions. Scheduled termination at 78% generally requires current payments. Appreciation-based removal follows separate servicer/investor rules; it is not automatic at 20% current equity. See the CFPB cancellation explanation before assuming a removal date.
Is FHA's minimum down payment also 3%?

No. Standard FHA maximum financing can allow 3.5% down for a qualifying borrower with a decision credit score of at least 580; other requirements and lender standards apply. The FHA guide explains why the insurance structure also needs a separate comparison.

This widget models a conventional loan with borrower-paid monthly PMI. At 20% down or more it sets that charge to zero. A zero-PMI assumption below 20% must be supported by your actual product; some alternatives shift costs into a rate or upfront fee.
